en: The Liturgy of Homage to the Dharma-body of the Buddha Praised by the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
together with its Preface; this liturgy is extracted from the *Mahāyāna-sarvaviṣayajñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra*.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery—honored with the title of Kai-fu-yi-tong-sansi, Tejin, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Sushan with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously titled Sikong, and conferred the posthumous name Dajian, with the honorary title Dayangzhi—by imperial decree. The Emperor governs the realm with profound benevolence.
The great brilliance illuminates all things;
it universally sprinkles nectar,
purifying and refreshing the common people.
I, Bukong, have unworthily basked in Your Majesty’s sacred compassion and have been improperly entrusted with the task of translation;
I now specifically receive this gracious imperial command.
He summoned sixteen eminent śramaṇas who were masters of the study of doctrine in the capital,
including Liangfen, and at the Inner Court,
completed the translation of the *Benevolent Kings' Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-guhyaka-alaṃkāra Sūtra*, and other scriptures.
Following the Prayer of Praise,
I pray that you may receive boundless blessings for your person, O Most Enlightened One.
I have humbly observed the *Sūtra on Praising the Dharmakāya of the Buddha Spoken by the Great Holy Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*.
According to its Sanskrit original, there are forty-one prostrations; however,
those practiced in previous traditions consist of only ten prostrations,
which are incomplete in their phrasing and lack fullness in their praise of virtues.
I fear that [otherwise] I would contravene the earnest sincerity of the Sage and deprive sentient beings of their supreme benefit.
Previously, I possessed a Sanskrit manuscript.
All [of these] are now complete and translated for circulation, so that they may contribute to the propagation and benefit [of the Dharma].
As for the remaining repentance rituals and procedures, they remain as in the original texts;
they will not be discussed further here.
At that time,
in the fourth month of summer, the first year of the Yongtai era of the Great Tang,
it was stated in the sutra:
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha,
together with a great assembly of twenty-five thousand bhikṣus.
All were arhats, together with seventy-two nayuta-koṭis of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
with Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva as their leader.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes,
bared his right shoulder, and prostrated at the feet of the Buddha.
With palms joined in reverence, he praised the Tathāgata by reciting these verses:
"Formless and without characteristics, Without sense faculties and without abode;
Because you are neither born nor extinguished, I pay homage to you who are beyond all objects of perception."
Neither going nor staying, neither grasping nor abandoning;
because of being far removed from the six sense bases, I pay homage to the one who has nothing to observe and does not dwell in any phenomena,
having transcended both existence and non-existence.
Because you act with equanimity, homage to you who are without objective reference;
because you have transcended the three realms, you are equal to space.
Because you are unstained by any desires, homage to you who are without objective reference.
Because you are always in a state of tranquility amidst all modes of conduct— whether going, coming, sleeping,
or waking— I pay homage to you who have no object of observation and for whom coming and going are entirely equal, having already abided in equanimity.
Homage to you who do not perceive objects, because you enter into signless meditative absorptions through the non-disruption of equanimity;
homage to you who do not perceive objects, because you see all phenomena as tranquil and always abide in samādhi.
Without abiding and without an object of observation, having attained mastery over phenomena through the power of wisdom that is ever-concentrated; I pay homage to the one who observes nothing,
who does not dwell upon the six sense faculties, and who is unattached to the six sense objects.
Because you always abide in the single characteristic, I pay homage to you who have no object of observation;
because you enter into the signless state, I pay homage to you who have no object of observation;
because you can sever all defilements and remain far removed from name-and-form, I pay homage to you who have no object of observation.
Not abiding in signs, yet free from all signs, entering the signless within the non-existent;
I pay homage to you who are without object of observation,
whose thought is non-conceptual, and whose mind dwells in the non-abiding.
Because no thoughts arise, I pay homage to the one who has nothing to observe;
To the one who is like space, without the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), Untainted, free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
and transcending the three times— I pay homage to the one who has nothing to observe.
Space has neither center nor periphery; the minds of all Buddhas are likewise so.
Because their minds are identical to space, I pay homage to those who have nothing to observe.
The Buddhas possess the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics.
Because you are free from all causes and effects, homage to you who have nothing to observe;
Because you do not cling to any phenomena, like the moon in water which cannot be grasped,
and because you are far removed from the mark of self, homage to you who have nothing to observe.
Not dwelling in the aggregates, not clinging to the sense bases or elements,
and being far removed from all inversions; I pay homage to you who have no object of observation and are ever equal to the dharmadhātu, having completely severed all views of a self.
Homage to you who are free from conceptual observation,
Who dwell nowhere among forms because you have distanced yourself from the two extremes; Neither grasping nor abandoning,
for you are far removed from what is not the Dharma— Homage to you who are free from conceptual observation.
You have realized the unobstructed Dharma, having attained penetration into all phenomena and being far removed from the ways of Māra; I pay homage to you who are without objective referent,
neither existent nor non-existent, and for whom existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
Homage to you who are beyond all verbal expression; Homage to you who are without an object of observation, who have shattered the banner of egoism.
Neither one nor two, because you are free from oneness and duality; Homage to you who are without an object of observation.
Body, speech, and mind are without fault; the three karmas are ever tranquil.
Because you are free from all metaphors, I pay homage to the All-Knowing One who abides eternally, manifesting through effortless spontaneity.

Homage to you who are free from all faults; Homage to you whose subtle, untainted mindfulness has no object of observation, And whose impartial mind, without limit or discrimination, regards both the sentient and the insentient.
Homage to you who have no object of observation.
Because the mind is unimpeded, you fully know all minds;
because they do not abide in self or other, I pay homage to the one who is without an object of observation,
who is unimpeded and without an object of observation, and who eternally abides in the unimpeded Dharma.
Because you are far removed from all mental states, I pay homage to you who have no object of observation.
Because your mind is always without an objective referent, its self-nature is ungraspable;
because it is equal and immeasurable, I pay homage to you who have no object of observation.
With a mind that has no basis, you perceive all buddha-fields;
because you know all sentient beings, you pay homage to the omniscience (*sarvajñā*) that does not observe any phenomena, which is ultimately non-existent.
Because the Buddha-mind is difficult to fathom, I pay homage to the one who has no object of observation;
All phenomena are like illusions, and like illusions they cannot be apprehended.
Because he is free from all illusory phenomena, I pay homage to the one who has no object of observation.
The Buddha always dwells in the world, yet is unstained by worldly dharmas;
because he is unstained by the world, I pay homage to the Omniscient One who is eternally present,
who has nothing upon which to rely, and whose sphere is the emptiness of emptiness.
Because verbal expressions are also empty, I pay homage to the one who has no object of observation;
Because you have attained the samādhi of non-conceptualization and sport with the supernatural powers of the illusion-like samādhi, I pay homage to the one who has no object of observation.
Neither one nor different, neither near nor far,
because you do not move from the Dharma; I pay homage to the One-Pointed Vajra Samādhi,
which is without object and achieves perfect awakening in a single instant.
Homage to you who have realized the absence of images;
Homage to you who do not observe any phenomena of the three times. Homage to you who have accomplished all skillful means and remain unmoving in nirvāṇa; Homage to you who do not observe anything.
Nirvāṇa is eternally unmoving; Because it has mastered the skillful means that transcend both this shore and the other shore,
I pay homage to the one who is without object of observation,
signless, and non-existent, Free from affliction and free from conceptual proliferation.
I pay homage to you who do not abide in existence or non-existence;

I pay homage to you whose wisdom is without object, for all things are equal, And who are tranquil and free from discrimination, because self and other are of one single nature. I pay homage to you who are without object.
I prostrate with equal reverence to all; there is no one to whom I do not prostrate, nor anyone to whom I do not prostrate.
A single prostration encompasses all sentient beings, for they all return to the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
Excellent, excellent!
You have now well explained that all dharmas, which are the merits of the Tathāgata, are originally pure.
Mañjuśrī, suppose there were a person.

To transform and guide all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm so that they become pratyekabuddhas is not as meritorious as for someone to hear of these virtues and believe and understand them with even a single thought-moment.
It exceeds that by hundreds of thousands of millions of times;
thus, through such successive progression, it is impossible to praise, illustrate, or calculate its magnitude,
as fully described in the original sūtra.
